cards.title: British colonial rule takes hold
cards.description: The East India Company expands its power through the victories at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764). In 1765 it gains revenue collection rights in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

cards.title: Punjab is annexed
cards.description: The East India Company annexes Punjab after the Second Sikh War, ending the Sikh kingdom’s sovereignty. Punjab lies in the northwestern subcontinent: its western and eastern regions would become parts of Pakistan and India in 1947. Lahore and Amritsar offer geographic points of reference.

cards.title: Uprising and Crown rule
cards.description: After the 1857 uprising, the British Crown takes control of the Company’s territories in 1858. Direct Crown government is known as the British Raj.

cards.title: Organization and representation
cards.description: The Indian National Congress is founded in 1885; the All-India Muslim League follows in 1906. The 1909 reforms introduce separate Muslim electorates: Muslim voters elect representatives to seats reserved for Muslims.
cards.editorialNote: A dedicated source for the Muslim League’s founding is still needed.

cards.title: Iqbal · Taranah-i-Hindi
cards.description: Muhammad Iqbal imagines India as a homeland shared across religious communities. Read this earlier poem alongside “Taranah-i-Milli” to consider the changing relationship between home, geography, and community.
cards.publication: First publication and edition not yet verified
cards.edition: Primary text and credited translation pending. No translated excerpt is displayed.

cards.title: Iqbal · Taranah-i-Milli
cards.description: Muhammad Iqbal imagines a Muslim community that crosses geographic boundaries. Compare the poem’s imagined community with his later discussion of political organization at Allahabad.
cards.composition: Circa 1910; primary edition and translation still under review
cards.edition: Primary text and credited translation pending. No translated excerpt is displayed.

cards.title: World War I
cards.description: Troops from British India serve on several fronts, including Europe, the Middle East, and East Africa. Their wartime service leads into the unsettled postwar years under the Raj.

cards.title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
cards.description: British troops fire on a gathering in Amritsar, Punjab. The date is commemorated by the Jallianwala Bagh National Memorial.

cards.title: Iqbal’s Allahabad Address
cards.description: In his presidential address to the Muslim League, Iqbal discusses political organization in Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India. Read this speech alongside the poem without treating poetry as a direct blueprint for a later border.

cards.title: World War II
cards.description: The British viceroy brings India into the war without consulting Indian political leaders. This war overlaps the Lahore Resolution and the Quit India movement.

cards.title: Lahore Resolution
cards.description: The Muslim League sets out demands for political arrangements in Muslim-majority regions. Return to Iqbal’s Allahabad Address to compare earlier political proposals.

cards.title: Quit India
cards.description: Congress calls for an end to British rule. The colonial government suppresses the movement and arrests its leaders.

cards.title: Cabinet Mission and escalating violence
cards.description: The Cabinet Mission attempts to reach a constitutional settlement. Communal violence escalates as negotiations over the transfer of power continue.

cards.title: Partition plan announced
cards.description: The plan sets out a transfer of power to two governments and the planned division of Punjab and Bengal.

cards.title: Independence celebrations
cards.description: Ceremonies take place in Karachi on August 14 and in New Delhi on August 15. These celebrations precede the public announcement of the boundary awards. Faiz’s damaged dawn asks what freedom has yet to deliver.

cards.title: Faiz · Freedom’s Dawn
cards.description: Faiz Ahmad Faiz’s damaged dawn and unfinished journey invite readers to consider the distance between independence and the freedom still being sought. This is a month-level date; no particular day is assigned.
cards.edition: English version translated by V. G. Kiernan. This card provides interpretation; the poem text is not reproduced.

cards.title: Radcliffe boundary awards made public
cards.description: The awards announce the borders through Punjab and Bengal. In Punjab, Lahore falls in Pakistan and Amritsar in India; Bengal is divided between West Bengal in India and East Bengal in Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The source includes a contemporary boundary map. Compare Auden’s later account of drawing the border.

cards.title: Displacement and violence in Punjab
cards.description: Across the Partition period, mass displacement and communal violence transform Punjab. Muslims move toward Pakistan; Sikhs and Hindus toward India. The span has no single end date. Pritam’s lament addresses the Punjabi poet Waris Shah through this shared landscape of loss.

cards.title: Pritam · To Waris Shah
cards.description: Amrita Pritam calls on Waris Shah, poet of the Punjabi romance Heer, to witness Punjab’s suffering. The reported composition date is distinct from the later English translation.
cards.publication: English translation published 1968–69 in Mahfil, pp. 27–28
cards.edition: Translated by Kiron Bajaj and Carlo Coppola.

cards.title: Auden · Partition
cards.description: W. H. Auden looks back at the drawing of the border from a later vantage point. This retrospective poem belongs to the memory of Partition as well as to the history of its boundaries.
cards.edition: Collected Poems, edited by Edward Mendelson, Modern Library, 2007, pp. 802–03.

cards.title: Gulzar · Footprints on Zero Line
cards.description: The English collection gathers writing on Partition and its continuing presence in memory. The individual poem remains open while “Eyes Don’t Need a Visa” and “Bhameri” are checked.
cards.edition: Translated by Rakhshanda Jalil; Harper Perennial, 2017. Individual selection pending.

poets.name: Muhammad Iqbal
poets.description: His poems ask what home meant before Partition. “Taranah-i-Hindi” imagines India as a shared homeland; “Taranah-i-Milli” turns toward a Muslim community that crosses borders.

poets.name: Faiz Ahmad Faiz
poets.description: His Urdu poem “Freedom’s Dawn” looks at independence through a dawn that falls short of what people hoped for.

poets.name: Amrita Pritam
poets.description: Her Punjabi poem “To Waris Shah” calls on an earlier Punjabi poet to witness the suffering of a divided Punjab. Waris Shah wrote Heer, a Punjabi romance rooted in the same landscape.

poets.name: W. H. Auden
poets.description: His poem “Partition” looks back at the drawing of the border through Cyril Radcliffe, the British official who chaired the boundary commissions.

poets.name: Gulzar
poets.description: His writing looks back on childhood displacement and explores how the border continues to shape memory. The individual poem selection remains open while the collection is checked.
